rows: Mount Omei, west of Kiatingfu, Szechuan (10,158 ft.). A pilgrim resort for Buddhists. L. Richard states that 56 pagodas have been erected on the mountain, the highest at an elevation of 10,000 ft. Mr. R. F. Johnston enumerates 35 monasteries or temples passed on a journey up and down the mountain.
The Three Peaks of Dokerla.—A centre of Tibetan pilgrimages. N.W. Yunnan (19,700 ft.).

Wu Tai Shan.—North of Shansi. The monastery on this mountain is said to be the oldest in China. It is visited annually by thousands of pilgrims, Chinese, Mongolian and Tibetan. The Dalai Lama stayed here on his return from Peking to Lhassa (1909).

table.title: [Chief Lakes of China Proper]
table.caption_extra: Lakes. Introduced in the text: 'The chief lakes of China Proper are :—'. Running heads 'OROGRAPHY—LAKES.' (p. 36) and 'LAKES—RIVERS.' (p. 37).

rows: The Tungting lake in Hunan. In summer, when it receives the overflow of the Yangtze, its dimensions reach 75 miles in length and 65 in breadth (2000 sq. miles); but in winter the lake empties its waters into the Yangtze and becomes merely an enormous marsh, with two main river channels passing through it, the Yuenkiang and Siangkiang. In 1910 the provincial authorities made a start of dredging the lake, a machine having been bought for that purpose in Germany. The dredger was manned and operated by a Chinese crew, and began work on the Changteh channel.
The Po-yang lake in Kiangsi; 90 miles by 20 (approx.). The water rises nearly 30 ft. in the flood season, when the area of the lake is approximately 1800 sq. miles.
The Tai-hu, or Great Lake, in Kiangsu, S. of the Yangtze. Its greatest dimensions are approximately 50 miles by 40 miles, but its waters recede in winter.
The Hungtseh lake in Kiangsu and Anhui, N. of the Yangtze, connected on the N.E. with the Grand Canal and on the S.E. with
The Kaoyiu lake, also in Kiangsu.
The Tatsung lake lies E. of the Kaoyiu, on the other side of the Grand Canal.
The Tien-hu lake in Yunnan, S. of Yunnanfu; approximately 38 miles in length and 8 in width and lying at an altitude of 6300 ft.
The Eulhai lake, also in Yunnan, E. of Talifu. It lies at an altitude of 6500 ft. above sea-level, but is slightly smaller than the Tien-hu.
Dalai-nor; Buir-nor, or Pir Lake; Lake Hinka (Khanka)
In Manchuria are to be found the Dalai-nor and Buir-nor, or Pir Lake, both S.W. of Hailar, and Lake Hinka (Khanka) in the extreme east of the province, W. of the Ussuri River.

table.title: [Principal Lakes of Tibet and Chinese Turkestan]
table.caption_extra: Lakes. Introduced in the text: 'In Tibet and Chinese Turkestan recent exploration has added largely to our knowledge of the lake system of these vast territories. Here it will suffice to enumerate the principal lakes.'

rows: Koko-nor, in N.E. Tibet near the borders of Kansu, 65 miles long and 40 wide, with an area of 2300 sq. miles. It lies at an altitude of 10,500 ft. above sea-level. Its waters are salt.
Tsaidam, west of the Koko-nor, now little more than a dreary swamp.

Lob-nor, north of the Altyn Tagh range. Between 1877 and the present day this once important expanse of water has diminished in size to an enormous extent. Of these three basins Dr. A. H. Keane says in Stanford's Compendium of Geography: “The gradual isolation of all these basins affords one of the most striking illustrations of the process of desiccation that has been going on throughout Central Asia from the remotest times. First the Koko-nor fails to reach the Tsaidam; then the Tsaidam ceases to communicate with Lob-nor and ultimately dries up, while Lob-nor sinks to a mere reedy morass some 3 or 4 feet deep.”
Kizil-Bash or Lake Ulungur, between the Tienshan and Altai Mountains.
Ike Aral-nor, — in the extreme west of Mongolia.
Ubsa-nor, — in the extreme west of Mongolia.
Lake Bogratch, south of the Bogdo-ola Mountains.
Kara-nor, in the Nan-shan (Mountains) north-west of Koko-nor.
Tengri-nor, north of Lhassa: altitude 15,000 ft.
